planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or very early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil.

directions: Red Dutch is among the oldest named red currant selections still grown today, with cultivation records tracing back to the late 1500s in the Low Countries. The upright, multi-stemmed bush produces long strigs of small, tart, bright red berries in midsummer, ripening slightly earlier than many modern hybrids. It tolerates light shade and prefers cool root conditions, making it well suited to northern gardens where summer heat is moderate. Prune out the oldest third of the wood each winter to keep the bush productive, since currants fruit best on two- and three-year-old stems.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or very early spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil.

directions: White Dutch is a translucent, pale-fruited sport of the red currant that has been grown in American and European gardens since colonial times, valued for its milder, sweeter flavor compared with red-fruited forms. The arching bush bears heavy clusters of pearly, almost golden berries in midsummer, which hang well on the plant without dropping. It performs best with afternoon shade in warmer zones and steady soil moisture through fruit development. Renewal-prune older canes each winter to maintain vigorous new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring into cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Redstart is a later-ripening red currant selection prized for its sturdy, upright growth and long strigs of bright, medium-sized berries that hang well into August rather than clustering all at once in early summer. This later harvest window helps extend the currant season and spreads out picking in a mixed small-fruit planting. The bush is notably productive and disease-resistant compared with older heirloom types, and tolerates the same cool, evenly moist conditions favored by other red currants. Thin out crowded interior canes in winter to maintain airflow and encourage strong new fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root bushes in fall or early spring in well-drained soil amended with compost.

directions: Keepsake is a British gooseberry selection known for its greenish-red fruit of good dessert quality and its role as a parent in the breeding of the disease-resistant cultivar Invicta. The thorny, spreading bush ripens its fruit in early to midsummer and bears well even on young plants. Grow it in cool, humus-rich soil with afternoon shade in hot climates, since gooseberries decline quickly under prolonged heat stress. Prune to an open goblet shape each winter, removing wood more than three years old to keep berries easy to reach past the thorns.
sources: ScienceDirect: Genetic diversity in gooseberry (Ribes uva-crispa)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into moist, well-drained soil; a second highbush cranberry nearby improves fruit set.

directions: Phillips is an upright, broad-growing selection of the native American highbush cranberry valued for setting heavy crops of fruit even on young plants, unlike many seedling-grown forms that take years to bear reliably. Flat lacecap clusters of white flowers in late spring give way to drooping clusters of glossy, wine-red berries that persist on the shrub well into winter, providing food for birds and a tart fruit used for sauces and jellies after a frost mellows the flavor. Fall foliage turns shades of burgundy and scarlet, adding ornamental value beyond the fruit display. Grow in full sun for the heaviest fruit set and prune only lightly, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.
sources: University of Wisconsin Cooperative Extension — Uncommon Fruit

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into well-drained soil; full fruiting output builds over several years.

directions: Cido is a thornless Japanese flowering quince selected specifically for fruit production rather than ornamental bloom, making harvest far easier than from the spiny wild species. Orange-red spring flowers are followed by hard, aromatic, yellow-green fruit that ripens in early fall and is notably high in vitamin C and pectin, prized across Scandinavia and the Baltics for juice, syrup, and jelly. The low, suckering shrub tolerates poor soil and drought once established and needs little care beyond occasional thinning of old wood. Fruit is inedible raw due to its hardness and tartness but cooks down easily into preserves.
